source: Leinonen et al. (2023) Using LLMs to enhance programming error messages
finding: Codex (code-davinci-002) was asked to explain Python error messages for novices. It nearly always produced an explanation, but often a wrong one.
numbers: 9 error messages x 3 programs x 3 Codex outputs. Explanation present 67-100% of cases; explanation correct 11% (unexpected EOF while parsing) to 83% (can't assign to function call). Fix present 44-89%; fix correct only 33% overall (17% to 56% by message).
limits: Two raters, qualitative; small set; 2022 model; Python only.
agent_relevance: Plain-language rewrite of tool output is easy for LLMs; correctness of the diagnosis is not. An agent should verify a model's reading of an error before acting on it.

source: Leinonen et al. (2023) Using LLMs to enhance programming error messages
finding: Prompt wording changed how often Codex gave an empty answer. Five prompt variants were tried and the best one was kept.
numbers: Empty responses out of 81 generated explanations: 4, 6, 7, 16, 27 for prompts 1 to 5.
limits: Only empty-response rate was used to pick the prompt, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Prompt choice shifts failure rate several-fold for the same task; tune the scaffold on a held-out metric.

source: Leinonen et al. (2023) Using LLMs to enhance programming error messages
finding: Authors frame LLM error explanation as the newest step in a six-decade effort to make compiler messages readable to novices ('enhanced error messages'). Earlier readability rewrites had been shown to help novices understand messages.
numbers: Background claim; cited prior work says readability rewrites raised understanding and successful corrections (no figure given in the text read).
limits: Background only; not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Tool output design for agents is the same problem: raw compiler text is written for experts.

source: Prather et al. (2023) 'It's weird that it knows what I want': novices and Copilot
finding: First observation study of CS1 students using Copilot. Novices showed new interaction patterns: shepherding (typing the suggestion out by hand) and backtracking (deleting just-accepted code).
numbers: Observation plus interview, 30-minute CS1 task (Minesweeper-style). 13 participants backtracked at least once, the fifth most frequent coded behaviour.
limits: Small qualitative sample, one assignment, one session, one institution.
agent_relevance: Accepting without reading is the main failure. A scaffold that forces a read-and-check step before using generated output targets this.

source: Prather et al. (2023) 'It's weird that it knows what I want'
finding: Large suggestion blocks overload novices; they spent time decoding code they did not write. Students reported both learning from suggestions and worry that typing practice is lost.
numbers: Participant P01 said most time went on decoding the code; 3 participants said a suggestion taught them something new. Themes: Interactions, Cognitive, Purpose, Speculation.
quote: You might have code that works but you have no idea how it works.
limits: Self-report; no learning test.
agent_relevance: Output size and explainability matter; smaller verified steps beat one big block.

source: Barke, James, Polikarpova (2022) Grounded Copilot: how programmers interact with code-generating models
finding: Grounded theory of Copilot use: two modes, acceleration (programmer knows what to write, tool saves typing) and exploration (programmer unsure, tool suggests a path). The authors link this to dual-process thinking.
numbers: 20 participants (15 academia, 5 industry), 9 had used Copilot before; tasks in four languages.
limits: Self-selected participants; 2022 tool; theory, not effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Agent could switch between a fast copy mode and a slow explore mode. In explore mode compare several alternatives and validate each.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on novice learners (CHI)
finding: Randomised controlled study of Codex for beginners aged 10-17. Codex helped during training and did not hurt manual coding afterwards.
numbers: 69 learners (Codex 33, Baseline 36), 45 tasks over 10 sessions. Authoring correctness 80.1% vs 44.4% (d=1.67, p<.001); time 210s vs 361s (d=1.56); completion 90.9% vs 79.0% (d=0.68, p=.006); documentation use 22.1% vs 54.3%; errors per task 1.28 vs 2.17.
limits: Ages 10-17; 21 of 90 dropped out; Codex-era model; Scratch pre-test matched (62.7% vs 60%).
agent_relevance: Assistance lifts task score a lot. Score during assisted work is not a measure of learning.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI code generators on novice learners (CHI)
finding: Learning after removing the tool: no significant difference. The Codex group was slightly better a week later but not significantly; it made more errors when no starter code was given.
numbers: Immediate post-test authoring 61.3% vs 62.9% (p=.838). Retention authoring 59.1% vs 49.8% (d=0.28, p=.262); modifying 47.5% vs 34.8% (d=0.41, p=.092). Errors on retention authoring 1.58 vs 0.99 (p=.042). Modifying task in training 66.2% vs 58.4% (p=.202). Learners with higher Scratch pre-test gained more.
limits: Underpowered for the retention effects; one week only. Contrasts with the adult skill-formation study (c15).
agent_relevance: Benefit depends on prior skill; heterogeneity matters for any claim that a scaffold helps.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) How novices use LLM-based code generators in a self-paced environment
finding: Log analysis of 33 learners and about 1,700 Codex prompts. Learners went to Codex first and often pasted the task text. Four coding approaches were found: AI Single Prompt, AI Step-by-Step, Hybrid, Manual.
numbers: Codex used at task start in 46% of prompts (n=760); 92% of those had no manual attempt first; 66% copied the full task description. 90% (75 of 83) of editor-clearing events followed an unsuccessful Codex use.
limits: Thematic coding, inter-rater agreement 0.87 on 13.2% of data; same sample as c07-c08.
agent_relevance: Decomposing into sub-goals (Step-by-Step) is a prompt-side scaffold learners used themselves; most did not.

source: Denny, Kumar, Giacaman (2023) Conversing with Copilot: prompt engineering for CS1 problems
finding: Copilot solved about half of 166 CS1 problems at first try. Rewording the problem in natural language rescued many of the rest.
numbers: 79 of 166 solved verbatim (47.6%). Of 87 unsolved, 53 solved after prompt edits (about 60%); 34 stayed unsolved. 15 'conceptual' problems with 6 specific concepts (for example swapping neighbours) failed every time.
limits: Manual rewording by authors, not by students; one model; CodeCheck dataset.
agent_relevance: Prompt repair adds missing specification. An agent can do a rewrite-the-spec step on failure; here it recovered about 60%.

source: Becker et al. (2023) Programming is hard - or at least it used to be
finding: Position paper: code-generating AI will change CS1 and CS2 teaching; community should act fast. Cites Finnie-Ansley: Codex outperformed most students on exams.
numbers: Codex repeated sampling raised pass rates to about 70% (cited from Chen et al.); AlphaCode in top 54% of 5,000+ contest entrants (as cited).
limits: Opinion and literature summary, no new data; numbers are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Background for why tool and language design for humans is now partly design for LLMs.

source: Peng et al. (2023) The impact of AI on developer productivity: evidence from GitHub Copilot
finding: Controlled trial: developers with Copilot finished an HTTP server task much faster.
numbers: 95 Upwork developers; JavaScript HTTP server; treated group 55.8% faster (95% CI 21-89%). Less experienced, older, and long-hours programmers gained most.
limits: Single small greenfield task; time to finish only; wide CI; control could use web search.
agent_relevance: Speed gains on clean tasks. Compare with c13 on realistic repos.

source: METR (2025) Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developers
finding: Randomised trial on real issues in mature repos: experts were slower with AI and believed they were faster.
numbers: 246 issues (136 AI-allowed, 110 AI-disallowed); AI increased completion time by 19%. Forecast before: 24% faster; belief after: 20% faster. Raw ratio 34%; regression 19% after adjusting issue difficulty. ML and economics experts also over-predicted speedup.
limits: 16 developers, early-2025 tools (Cursor Pro), own repos; may not generalise.
agent_relevance: Self-assessed speedup is unreliable. An agent loop needs measured checks, not its own judgement of progress.

source: Perry et al. (2023) Do users write more insecure code with AI assistants?
finding: With an AI assistant participants wrote less secure code and felt more sure it was secure.
numbers: 47 participants, five security tasks in Python, JavaScript, C. Encryption task: 67% correct with AI vs 79% control, more insecure answers (p=0.017). Signing task: 3% secure with AI vs 21% (p=0.039). SQL task: 36% of AI group vulnerable to injection vs 7% of control.
limits: Small N; per-task tests; Codex-based assistant; confidence is self-report.
agent_relevance: Over-trust in tool output. Add a security and correctness check step; do not let model self-rating gate.

source: Shen and Tamkin (2026) How AI impacts skill formation
finding: Randomised trial: learning a new Python library (Trio) with an AI assistant cut quiz scores but did not clearly save time.
numbers: 52 participants (26 per group), 27-point quiz on concepts, code reading, debugging. Quiz effect Cohen d=0.738, p=0.01, a 4.15-point mean gap (about 50% vs 65% per web summary). Task time p=0.391 (AI about 23 min vs 25).
limits: Single session, one library, small N; writing questions excluded. Some d and p values elsewhere in the paper come from pilots.
agent_relevance: Offloading lowers learning even when speed is flat. Shows why scaffolds that keep the human reasoning matter.

source: Shen and Tamkin (2026) How AI impacts skill formation
finding: Six AI-use patterns. Low scorers delegated code or debugging to AI. High scorers asked conceptual questions or asked for explanations with code.
numbers: Low patterns scored under 40% (24%-39%); high patterns 65% or higher. Patterns include AI Delegation, Progressive AI Reliance, Iterative AI Debugging (low); Conceptual Inquiry and Hybrid Code-Explanation (high). Manual copying of AI code differed from pasting.
limits: Exploratory clustering after the trial, not randomised.
agent_relevance: A prompt style, ask for why rather than the code, is a candidate scaffold rule for an agent teaching or reasoning loop.

source: Lehmann, Cornelius, Sting (2025) AI meets the classroom: when do LLMs harm learning?
finding: Two preregistered lab experiments found no overall effect of LLMs on learning. Effect depends on use: substituting (generating solutions) trades depth for coverage; complementing (asking explanations) raises understanding.
numbers: Field study 6,594 observations in two graduate programming courses; two lab experiments with a 45-minute Python lesson (24 parts). LLMs widen the gap between low and high prior knowledge.
limits: Usage-behaviour split is exploratory; lab subjects were students with little Python.
agent_relevance: Consistent with c15 and c16: how the model is used decides the outcome. Skill gap matters.

source: Prather et al. (2024) The widening gap: benefits and harms of generative AI for novice programmers
finding: Replication of a 31-student metacognition study with GenAI added. Students who were already strong accelerated; strugglers kept old metacognitive errors and gained new ones.
numbers: 21 lab sessions with observation, interview and Tobii eye tracking; 20 of 21 finished the problem. Original study n=31.
limits: Small N; qualitative; one problem.
agent_relevance: Tools help the expert more; an agent scaffold should expose a check on its own progress, since false sense of progress is the known novice error.

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp: LLMs with guardrails for scalable support in programming classes
finding: A deployed LLM help tool for classes that refuses to give solution code. Three prompt stages: sufficiency check of the question, main answer, then a second LLM pass to strip code blocks.
numbers: Authors note models are strongly biased to give full solutions even when told not to, so a separate code-removal prompt is needed. Deployed for 12 weeks.
limits: Reports usage and student reception, not learning gains.
agent_relevance: Guardrail by a second pass beats instruction alone. Reusable loop step: draft, check against a rule, repair.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2024) CodeAid: classroom deployment of an LLM programming assistant
finding: 12-week deployment in a C systems course with about 700 students. Assistant gave pseudo-code and conceptual help but not code.
numbers: More than 8,000 interactions logged; 563 survey participants; interviews with 22 students; one response-quality rating of 94% (alpha .92), others 87% and 82%. Midway change: Help Fix Code first generates correct code then suggests fixes, which improved suggestion quality.
limits: Self-reported usefulness; students were barred from other AI tools; the 94/87/82 rating labels were not fully read.
agent_relevance: Generating a correct reference internally then explaining the diff is a useful hidden step.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: agent-computer interfaces enable automated software engineering
finding: Tool design for an LM agent matters like usability for a human. A purpose-built interface (viewer, editor, search) beat a plain Linux shell.
numbers: Principles: simple actions, compact actions, informative feedback, guardrails. Evaluated on SWE-bench (2,294 tasks), ablations on Lite; full design 18.0% on Lite with GPT-4 Turbo.
limits: Ablations on one model, Lite subset; table shows run deltas.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as human-factors: usability of the tool for the thinker changes outcomes. A core method of this subfield now used in agent loops.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent ablations
finding: Each interface part removed lowered the resolve rate. Edit with linting guardrail 18.0 vs no edit action 10.3 (-7.7). Search: summarized 18.0, iterative 12.0 (-6.0), no search 15.7 (-2.3). File viewer: 100 lines 18.0, 30 lines 14.3 (-3.7), full file 12.7 (-5.3). Context: last 5 observations 18.0, full history 15.0, without demo 16.3.
numbers: Percent resolved on SWE-bench Lite, GPT-4 Turbo, 6 runs. Of 135 edit-failure cases in resolved trajectories, the agent recovered 104 times.
limits: Interactions may not be additive; one benchmark; model snapshots shift.
agent_relevance: Window size and linting echo human usability: too little or too much hurts. Immediate error feedback (lint) is a guardrail an agent loop should copy.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: human UIs are not agent UIs
finding: Chains of cd, ls, cat exploration are inefficient for LMs; grep or find do better; silent edits with no feedback confuse models and raise error risk.
numbers: Qualitative case studies plus the ablation table.
quote: Human user interfaces are not always suitable as agent-computer interfaces.
limits: Anecdotal parts.
agent_relevance: Do not hand an agent the raw human tool set; shape it.

source: Finnie-Ansley et al. (2022) The robots are coming: Codex and introductory programming
finding: Reported second-hand in c10 and c11: Codex scored in the 75th percentile of students on CS1 exam questions and solved about half of questions on the first attempt.
numbers: 75th percentile; roughly half at first attempt (as cited by Denny et al.).
limits: Second-hand; not opened.
agent_relevance: Baseline for model versus student comparisons.

source: Sarsa et al. (2022) Automatic generation of programming exercises and code explanations using LLMs
finding: Cited in the Copilot papers read: over 80% of Codex-generated exercises had executable sample solutions, but the solution passed Codex's own generated tests only about 30% of the time. Explanations: all parts covered in 90% of cases, only 70% of lines correct.
limits: Second-hand; not opened.
agent_relevance: Self-written tests are a weak check on self-written code.

source: Prather et al. (2023) The robots are here: generative AI in computing education
finding: Working-group report on how generative AI changes computing education. Not opened this session.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Not opened; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Context only.
